newsitem.title: CHINA: Foreign funds can help China market mature-Mobius.
newsitem.headline: Foreign funds can help China market mature-Mobius.

text.p: Allowing foreign mutual funds to set up shop in China will bring stability to the country's stock markets by encouraging investors to take long-term positions, investment guru Mark Mobius predicted.
"I think it would lower the volatility substantially," he said in an interview late on Tuesday.
"It would lower the risk the government now runs with people speculating in the markets and then maybe running to the government and asking for compensation," he said.
"We spend a lot of time and money on education which would help market maturity," he added.
Mobius, who controls more than $10 billion in equity funds, is in Shanghai to complete the purchase of a new southeast Asian headquarters for his company, Templeton Emerging Markets Fund Inc.

Templeton is viewed as a front-runner to become one of the first foreign companies to establish mutual funds based on the Chinese stock markets, known for their volatility and the preference of investors for short-term speculative plays.
On the potential size of the Chinese mutual fund market, Mobius said: "The sky's the limit.
"But in terms of what we can expect at the beginning, I'd say it's very small. You've got to explain and educate, what is a stock, why you have to be patient, why you have to be long-term," he said.
China launched domestic mutual funds in the early 1990s, soon after the country's two stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen were set up.
The experiment has been largely unsuccessful so far, with most losing money.
The funds make up less than one percent of the total stock holdings and volume on the Chinese markets, in dramatic contrast to the position of such funds on most markets around the world.
Mobius said that in the early stages, the foreign-managed funds would be domestic only, allowing Chinese investors to buy the local currency A shares.
"This is very similar to what we're doing in Russia where we're establishing a fund for investment by Russians in Russian stocks," he said.

"But eventually, it makes sense for us to have global funds, because that's really where we can contribute to the financial well-being of the people here. The more they diversify globally, the better off they will be," he said.
Templeton on Tuesday bought a whole floor of the new Shanghai stock exchange building and expects to move in in August, Mobius said.
China is expected to promulgate new regulations on the mutual fund industry later this year, but Mobius said there was no clear indication of when foreign funds could start operations.
"It really depends on the government," he said. "But we could be sitting here for quite a few years. We'll put our name on the list and hopefully we'll get in here sooner rather than later."
Mobius said he was "selectively bullish" on the Chinese foreign currency-denominated B share firms listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen.
"We're seeing the reforms coming through in these companies. You're seeing the transformation of these state dinosaurs into more mature, modern, rational companies," he said.
